title: The Swan and the Timetable: an Imperial Ballerina Against the Map
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, birth to a laundress
stops.date_confidence: attested: 31 January Julian, 12 February Gregorian (Wikipedia; Encyclopedia.com). Birthplace unsettled: Wikipedia gives Saint Petersburg proper, the Preobrazhensky Regiment hospital; Keith Money and most reference works give the village of Ligovo outside the city. Not reconciled here.
stops.campa: In the last winter of Alexander II's reign a laundress named Lyubov Fyodorovna Pavlova bears a daughter and registers her under the surname of a soldier, Matvey Pavlov, who is briefly her husband. The child is small, born early by the family's account, and reared on the thin means of a woman who washes other people's linen. Who her father was is argued over for a century; the name of a Jewish banker, Lazar Polyakov, circulates through the biographies and is never proved. She is Anna Matveyevna, and she grows up poor at the edge of the imperial capital.
suggested_refs: Parish registration of Anna Matveyevna Pavlova, Saint Petersburg, 1881
Keith Money, Anna Pavlova: Her Life and Art (1982), on the Ligovo birthplace tradition
sources: Keith Money, Anna Pavlova: Her Life and Art (1982)

stops.name: Mariinsky Theatre, the child at The Sleeping Beauty
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (Wikipedia); the Petipa production premiered January 1890 and she is generally said to have attended later that year. Sources give her age as nine; some popular accounts say eight.
stops.campa: Her mother buys two seats at the Mariinsky and takes her to Tchaikovsky's The Sleeping Beauty, staged by Marius Petipa for the imperial theatres. Gilded tiers, an orchestra of sixty, the Lilac Fairy crossing the stage on a car of flowers: the child watches the whole evening without moving in her seat. Walking home she tells her mother that she means to dance the part of Aurora in that theatre. The mother laughs. The girl does not, and repeats it until it is arranged that she be taken to the school on Theatre Street to be looked at by the examiners.
suggested_refs: Petipa's 1890 Mariinsky production of Tchaikovsky's The Sleeping Beauty

stops.name: Imperial Theatrical School, Rossi Street, the admission
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia): rejected at a first audition as too young and frail, admitted at ten in 1891. The atlas pin for the school is the shared Saint Petersburg coordinate carried by the Balanchine and Nijinsky files; the true geocode of 2 Rossi Street is 59.9303, 30.3358.
stops.campa: She is brought before the examiners of the Imperial Theatrical School and refused: too young, too thin, a chest the doctors distrust. She waits, is brought again, and at ten is taken in. The school is a closed world of uniforms, prayers, ranked dormitories and long days at the barre, run for the court and paid for out of the crown's purse. Behind the yellow walls of Rossi Street she is fed, housed, taught French and taught to dance, and a pupil who enters on those terms owes the imperial theatres the length of her career.
suggested_refs: The Imperial Theatrical School, 2 Rossi Street, now the Vaganova Academy

stops.name: Rossi Street, the broom and Gerdt's rage
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the nicknames, the teachers, and the fouette episode are biographical tradition repeated by Wikipedia without documentary anchor. Entry into Ekaterina Vazem's classe de perfection in 1898 is attested. The Gerdt speech is set at no dated occasion in any source.
stops.campa: The other girls call her the broom, for her thinness, and la petite sauvage. Her feet are high-arched and her ankles weak, exactly the build that the reigning Italian technique of multiple turns punishes. She studies under Christian Johansson, Pavel Gerdt, Nikolai Legat and later Enrico Cecchetti, and in her last year enters Ekaterina Vazem's classe de perfection. Attempting the thirty-two fouettes that made Pierina Legnani's name, she brings Gerdt to fury. He tells her that the frailty she is trying to drill out of herself is the whole of her gift.
stops.quote: ... leave acrobatics to others. It is positively more than I can bear to see the pressure such steps put on your delicate muscles and the severe arch of your foot. I beg you to never again try to imitate those who are physically stronger than you. You must realize that your daintiness and fragility are your greatest assets. You should always do the kind of dancing which brings out your own rare qualities instead of trying to win praise by mere acrobatic tricks.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Pavel Gerdt, addressing Pavlova at the Imperial Ballet School; blockquoted, and uncited, in the English Wikipedia article 'Anna Pavlova'
suggested_refs: Ekaterina Vazem's classe de perfection at the Imperial Theatrical School

stops.name: Mariinsky Theatre, the debut in Les Dryades pretendues
stops.date_confidence: attested: Encyclopedia.com dates the Maryinsky debut 19 September 1899; Wikipedia gives graduation at eighteen and entry as coryphee. One geography note in the research pool gives April 1899, which conflates the spring graduation with the September debut.
stops.campa: She graduates at eighteen and is not sent into the corps de ballet. The Imperial Ballet takes her directly as coryphee, and in September she appears at the Mariinsky in Pavel Gerdt's Les Dryades pretendues, before an audience that includes the balletomanes of the capital, men who keep records of every debut the way gamblers keep form. They mark her at once: light, unmuscular, weightless in a way the Italian school does not teach and has not managed to punish out of her.
suggested_refs: Mariinsky Theatre performance registers, season 1899-1900

stops.name: Mariinsky Theatre, the climb through the ranks
stops.date_confidence: attested for the promotions (Wikipedia): danseuse 1902, premiere danseuse 1905. The Fokine acquaintance in these years is tradition, undated.
stops.campa: Danseuse in 1902, premiere danseuse in 1905: she climbs the imperial ladder in the years when the ladder still governs everything, when rank is fixed by the director of the theatres and roles are assigned by decree. She takes Giselle, Paquita, La Bayadere, the Petipa repertory that has ruled this stage for forty years. Offstage she keeps company with a young choreographer, Mikhail Fokine, who argues that the whole apparatus of tutus, ranks and thirty-two fouettes has become a machine for counting rather than for dancing.
stops.quote: No one can arrive from being talented alone. God gives talent, work transforms talent into genius.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Anna Pavlova; cited via Yona Zeldis McDonough, 'Yes, These Famous Ballerinas Are Jewish,' Lilith, 3 November 2016, as quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Anna Pavlova'
suggested_refs: Imperial Theatres rank lists, Saint Petersburg, 1902-1905

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, the barefoot American
stops.date_confidence: attested in the isadora_duncan file for 28 January 1905; the sergei_diaghilev file places the same evening in the weeks after Bloody Sunday without fixing the date. Pavlova is named among the watchers in both.
stops.campa: An American dancer comes to Petersburg and performs barefoot, in a loose tunic, without pointe shoes, to concert music nobody has thought danceable. Isadora Duncan holds the hall. In the seats are Sergei Diaghilev, Fokine, Kschessinska and Pavlova, the whole of the imperial ballet's next twenty years sitting in the dark while its grammar is loosened in one evening. Fokine takes from it what he already suspected. Pavlova takes something else: that a dancer can stand alone on a stage, with no company behind her, and hold a house.
suggested_refs: Isadora Duncan's first Saint Petersburg season, January 1905

stops.name: Mariinsky Theatre, prima ballerina after Giselle
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the elevation following a Giselle (Wikipedia); the exact performance date is not given in any consulted source.
stops.campa: She dances Giselle, the mad scene and the graveyard act, and the theatre raises her to prima ballerina. She is twenty-five. The role asks for exactly what she has, a body that seems to weigh nothing in the second act and everything in the first, and asks nothing of what she lacks. The rank makes her first woman of the imperial stage, with the salary, the benefit performances and the claim on the repertory that come with it. Within four years she will leave all of it for music halls, steamships and towns with one theatre.
suggested_refs: Mariinsky production of Giselle in the Petipa staging, season 1905-1906

stops.name: Hall of the Noble Assembly, the four minutes of the swan
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Wikipedia's own article contradicts itself: the body text gives creation in 1905, the infobox gives a 1907 premiere. The standard reference date for the first documented performance is 22 December 1907, at a charity gala in this hall. The single-rehearsal story comes from Fokine's memoir and is self-reported.
stops.campa: Fokine makes her a solo of four minutes to the cello of Saint-Saens, Le Cygne from the Carnival of the Animals, and by his own account makes it almost in one pass, the dancer moving and the choreographer following. She performs it at a charity gala in the hall of the Noble Assembly. There is no story in it: a bird crosses the stage on small continuous steps, falters, folds. She will dance it some four thousand times over the next twenty-four years, in opera houses and tents and railway towns, and it outlives every full-length ballet she ever learns.
suggested_refs: The Hall of the Noble Assembly, now the Saint Petersburg Philharmonia
Fokine's memoirs on the making of The Dying Swan
sources: Keith Money, Anna Pavlova: Her Life and Art (1982)

stops.name: Bolshoi Theatre, Moscow, the first tour
stops.date_confidence: attested by Encyclopedia.com for a first Imperial Ballet tour to Moscow in 1907; the Bolshoi as venue is reconstruction from the routine exchange of principals between the two imperial stages, with no dated appearance confirmed.
stops.campa: She takes the company to Moscow, the first tour the Imperial Ballet makes to the rival capital with her name at the head of the bill. The Moscow house is larger than the Mariinsky and its audience is less schooled; what the Petersburg balletomanes would call coarse taste fills every seat. Moscow comes for her name rather than for the Imperial Ballet's, and the lesson is not lost on her. Dancing does not have to happen inside a court theatre, and a town with no ballet tradition of its own will pay to see one dancer twice.
suggested_refs: Imperial Theatres exchange of principal dancers between Saint Petersburg and Moscow

stops.name: Theatre du Chatelet, the first Saison Russe
stops.date_confidence: attested: the sergei_diaghilev file dates the opening 19 May 1909 and names Karsavina, Pavlova and Nijinsky as the three principal bodies of the season.
stops.campa: Sergei Diaghilev opens his first Saison Russe at the Chatelet with Le Pavillon d'Armide, the Polovtsian dances and Le Festin: Fokine choreographing, Benois and Bakst designing, and three names on the posters, Karsavina, Vaslav Nijinsky, Pavlova. Paris has not seen Russian dancing at this scale and loses its head over it. Serov draws her for the season's poster, the image that fixes her face across Europe. She dances the season and does not stay. The enterprise is Diaghilev's, and she has no wish to be one figure inside another man's design.
suggested_refs: Valentin Serov's 1909 poster of Pavlova for the Saison Russe
Theatre du Chatelet programmes, May-June 1909

stops.name: Paris, the Firebird refused
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance (Wikipedia): she was cast to lead Fokine's The Firebird, refused over Stravinsky's score, and the role went to Tamara Karsavina. The date belongs to the 1909-1910 preparation period; the ballet premiered 25 June 1910, so the pool's 1909 anchor is misleading.
stops.campa: Fokine builds The Firebird around her and she refuses it. The score is Stravinsky's, jagged and unmetrical to an ear trained on Minkus and Drigo, and she cannot hear the dance in it. The role passes to Tamara Karsavina and makes both the Ballets Russes and the century's new music. Pavlova walks the other way, into a repertory of short lyric pieces, national dances and abridged classics, work she can carry by ship into a town with a single theatre and an orchestra hired for the week.
suggested_refs: Fokine's The Firebird, premiered at the Paris Opera, 25 June 1910

stops.name: Metropolitan Opera House, New York, the American debut
stops.date_confidence: attested by Encyclopedia.com for February 1910 at the Metropolitan Opera House with Mikhail Mordkin; the exact night is not given in the consulted sources.
stops.campa: She lands in New York with Mikhail Mordkin and dances at the Metropolitan Opera House, after the opera, as a divertissement at the end of a long evening. The house has come for the singers and stays for the two Russians. American critics reach for the only vocabulary they have, which is the vocabulary of prodigy and of nature, and print it in every paper in the city. Ballet in the United States has been a novelty item on variety bills. Within a decade it is whatever Pavlova is doing, because for most of the country she is the only one doing it.
stops.quote: A generation of dancers turned to the art because of her. She roused America as no one had done since Elssler.
stops.quote_source: Agnes de Mille, The Book of the Dance (1963), p. 151, as quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Anna Pavlova'
suggested_refs: Metropolitan Opera performance archive, February 1910

stops.name: Palace Theatre, London, the variety bill
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Wikipedia's Palace Theatre article confirms Pavlova as one of Alfred Butt's attractions but gives no year; the engagement is usually placed in April 1910, and the research pool's March 1910 date is unsourced.
stops.campa: She takes an engagement at the Palace, a variety house on Cambridge Circus, billed between acrobats and comic singers at a salary no opera house pays. The balletomanes of Petersburg would call it a fall. She calls it an audience: two shows a day, working people in the cheap seats, a run that goes on for months and makes her the best-known dancer in England. Alfred Butt lists her among his attractions. London does not treat her as a curiosity shipped in from a court theatre; it treats her as a fixture, and she keeps coming back.
suggested_refs: Alfred Butt's variety bills at the Palace Theatre, Cambridge Circus, 1910

stops.name: London, a company of her own
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no consulted source pins the year. The research pool contradicts itself three ways, giving 1910, 1911, and a March 1910 Palace opening already under her own management. Range c.1910-1911. The company name Ballets Russes de Anna Pavlova could not be confirmed anywhere; her American billing was generally Anna Pavlova and her Ballet Russe.
stops.campa: She breaks with Diaghilev's enterprise and forms a company of her own, with Victor Dandre handling the money, the routes and the contracts, and puts it on the road. No opera house holds her. The company travels with its own scenery, its own conductor and a repertory that can be cut to fit any stage in any town. From this point until she dies she is almost never off tour. The dancers are drawn largely from England and Poland, drilled by Pavlova herself and by Enrico Cecchetti, and they follow her itinerary for years at a stretch.
stops.quote: A very enterprising and daring act. She toured on her own... for twenty years until her death. She traveled everywhere in the world that travel was possible, and introduced the ballet to millions who had never seen any form of Western dancing.
stops.quote_source: Agnes de Mille, The Book of the Dance (1963), p. 149, as quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Anna Pavlova'
suggested_refs: Touring contracts and billing of Anna Pavlova and her Ballet Russe
sources: Agnes de Mille, The Book of the Dance (1963)

stops.name: Ivy House, Golders Green, the lake and the swans
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1912 and for the residence lasting until her death (Wikipedia; English Heritage blue plaque). Coordinates corrected to the geocode of 94-96 North End Road NW11 7SX; the research pool carried three different and mutually inconsistent Ivy House pins.
stops.campa: She takes Ivy House on North End Road at Golders Green, a Georgian house with a garden and an ornamental lake, and keeps live swans on the water. It is the only address she holds for the rest of her life, and she is hardly ever inside it. She builds a studio in the house and works in it between tours, watching the birds on the lake for the solo she is asked for in every town she plays. She is photographed on the grass in a white dress with a swan in her arms, and the photograph travels further than she does.
suggested_refs: English Heritage blue plaque, Ivy House, North End Road, Golders Green
sources: English Heritage blue plaque record for Ivy House

stops.name: Auditorium Theatre, Chicago, the transcontinental years
stops.date_confidence: attested that near-annual coast-to-coast United States tours run from 1912 through 1926 (Wikipedia). Chicago as a regular stop is reconstruction from general touring itineraries; no specific Auditorium date was confirmed.
stops.campa: The company crosses the United States by train, season after season, playing Chicago, Cleveland, Kansas City and towns whose theatres have never held an orchestra pit. She dances in opera houses and in halls with an upright piano; where the stage is too small she cuts the corps and dances alone. The American tours run almost every year to 1926 and pay for everything else: the London house, the salaries, the passages to countries where no company can make money. She is the security on every loan the tours require.
suggested_refs: American touring itineraries of Anna Pavlova and her company, 1912-1926
sources: Keith Money, Anna Pavlova: Her Life and Art (1982)

stops.name: St Louis, the engagement at 5,500 dollars
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, citing St Louis engagement records) for a last-minute engagement arranged by the impresario Hattie B. Gooding at a reported expense of 5,500 dollars; month and day not given.
stops.campa: The impresario Hattie B. Gooding brings her to St Louis at short notice, at a reported expense of five thousand five hundred dollars. That is what one Pavlova evening costs an American city in 1914, and it is the figure the engagement records keep. She travels with a company, a conductor, trunks of costume and a schedule that allows one night in most towns. She is the draw and she is the collateral, and on a night when she does not appear nobody in the building is paid.
suggested_refs: Records of the Hattie B. Gooding St Louis engagement, 1914

stops.name: London, the marriage kept quiet
stops.date_confidence: attested that she married Victor Dandre in 1914 and that the marriage was kept private for years (Wikipedia); the place is given only as probably London, and the date within the year is not recorded in the consulted sources.
stops.campa: She marries Victor Dandre, who has booked her tours and kept her accounts since she left the Imperial Ballet, and the marriage stays private long after the fact. In public he remains her manager; the company calls him that and the programmes print it. No wedding record has been produced, and the sources give the place only as probably London. She is thirty-three and has not had a settled season since 1910. Dandre outlives her by thirteen years and writes the memoir from which nearly everything intimate about her is afterwards quoted.
suggested_refs: Victor Dandre, Anna Pavlova in Art & Life (London, 1932)
sources: Victor Dandre, Anna Pavlova in Art & Life (1932)

stops.name: Berlin, the war closes the road home
stops.date_confidence: attested by Encyclopedia.com that her last visit to Russia falls in 1914 and that she was stranded in Germany, and abroad thereafter, at the outbreak of the war. The specific city and date within the summer are not given; Berlin stands here for the German leg.
stops.campa: She goes back to Russia for the last time and does not know it is the last. The war finds her outside the country, in Germany, with her company scattered and the borders shutting behind her. She never sees Petersburg again. The school, the Mariinsky, the ranks and the benefit nights belong to a state that will not exist in four years. From here the touring stops being a strategy and becomes a condition of life: everything she owns moves with her, and the country that trained her is a place she can describe and cannot enter.
suggested_refs: Pavlova's final Russian visit, 1914

stops.name: Universal City, the only film
stops.date_confidence: attested: The Dumb Girl of Portici was shot in 1915 and released 3 April 1916 by Universal, directed by Lois Weber and Phillips Smalley. The research pool's 1915 release date is wrong. It is her only feature film.
stops.campa: Universal brings her to California, and Lois Weber and Phillips Smalley film her as Fenella, the mute girl of Portici, in a silent feature built out of Auber's opera. She acts far more than she dances; the camera cannot hold what she does with her arms and she knows it. The picture is released in 1916 and is the only feature she ever makes, and most prints are lost for decades afterward. The dancer whose whole reputation rests on being seen leaves behind a few minutes of usable film and a shelf of photographs.
suggested_refs: The Dumb Girl of Portici (Universal, 1916), directed by Lois Weber and Phillips Smalley

stops.name: New York, the fifty-minute Sleeping Beauty
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1916 (Wikipedia): an abridged version of The Sleeping Beauty of roughly fifty minutes, mounted in New York. Venue and exact dates are not given in the consulted sources.
stops.campa: In New York she stages The Sleeping Beauty, the ballet she watched as a child from a seat her mother paid for, cut to about fifty minutes for a house that will not sit through four acts of Petipa. She dances Aurora, the role she told her mother she would dance, twenty-six years after saying so. The cutting scandalises nobody present, because almost nobody in the theatre has seen the whole work. For most of the United States this is the first sight of any part of the imperial repertory.
suggested_refs: Pavlova's abridged Sleeping Beauty, New York, 1916

stops.name: Teatro Colon, Buenos Aires, the season on the other hemisphere
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The two sources conflict: Wikipedia states that in 1918-1919 her company toured throughout South America, Encyclopedia.com gives 1917. Span here taken as 1917-1919. The Colon as venue is recorded in the theatre's historical performance tradition but not confirmed against a dated programme.
stops.campa: The company crosses to Buenos Aires and plays the Teatro Colon, a house the size of the great European opera theatres, raised by a city that means to be counted among them. South America is not a stop on her route; it is a season, months of it, Argentina and Brazil and the Pacific coast, at a period when European companies treat the whole continent as too far to be worth the crossing. The crossing takes weeks and lands her in a summer that runs against the European calendar. The houses are full, and she books the continent again.
suggested_refs: Teatro Colon historical performance records, 1917-1919

stops.name: Teatro Municipal, Lima, the boy in the house
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance: Wikipedia records that Frederick Ashton, born 1904, resolved to become a choreographer after seeing Pavlova dance in Lima at the age of thirteen, which independently places a Lima performance around 1917. The venue is reconstruction.
stops.campa: She plays Lima on the Pacific leg, and somewhere in the house sits a thirteen-year-old English boy whose family is posted to Peru. Frederick Ashton watches her and decides on the spot what he will do with his life; he becomes the choreographer who shapes English ballet for the next fifty years. She never learns he was there. Nothing about the evening is arranged for him: he buys a seat in a country with no ballet company of its own, and watches a full programme danced as it would be danced in London.
suggested_refs: Frederick Ashton's account of seeing Pavlova dance in Lima

stops.name: Theatro Municipal, Rio de Janeiro, the tropics and the swan
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Brazilian leg is referenced in general accounts of her South American tours, and Wikipedia dates the tour 1918-1919 against Encyclopedia.com's 1917. The Theatro Municipal appearance is not confirmed against a dated programme.
stops.campa: The company plays the Theatro Municipal in Rio de Janeiro, a Paris opera house built in the tropics twenty years earlier and still without a resident ballet of its own. She brings hers: dancers, conductor, scenery and a programme of short pieces that ends, as every programme ends, with the swan. The season is the closest thing to a company the house has had. Reviewers describe an audience standing at the end, which by now happens in every port and is written down almost nowhere.
suggested_refs: Theatro Municipal do Rio de Janeiro programmes, 1918-1919

stops.name: Salvador da Bahia, the coast in the heat
stops.date_confidence: attested by Encyclopedia.com, which names Bahia and Salvador among Brazilian dates in 1919; Wikipedia's dating of the South American tour to 1918-1919 is compatible, its 1917 alternative in Encyclopedia.com is not. Contradiction left open.
stops.campa: The route runs north up the Brazilian coast to Bahia and Salvador, where the theatres are smaller, the heat spoils the rosin and the company has been travelling for the better part of a year. She dances the same programme she danced at the Colon. The rule she keeps until the last month of her life is that the town gets the whole evening: no shortened bill for a small house, no second dancer substituted for the swan. Those who tour with her describe one-night stands and night trains running for months without a rest week.
suggested_refs: Encyclopedia.com chronology of the 1919 Brazilian dates

stops.name: Saint-Cloud, the house of orphans
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia) that she supported Russian orphan girls displaced by the Revolution and Civil War and established a home for about fifteen of them near Saint-Cloud; the founding date within the period is not precisely given.
stops.campa: Out of the wreck of the Russian civil war she takes in fifteen girls, orphans of the emigration, and sets them up in a house at Saint-Cloud outside Paris with a matron and a schoolmistress, paid for out of the tours. Some of them she trains herself. She is by now the highest-earning dancer in the world and the money leaves as fast as it arrives: the house, the school, the relief funds for Russian refugees, the payroll of a company of forty people who have no other employer. She was a laundress's daughter in a rented room.
suggested_refs: Pavlova's orphanage for Russian refugee girls at Saint-Cloud

stops.name: Royal Opera House, Bombay, the borrowed vocabulary
stops.date_confidence: attested that the company toured India and that Indian dance observed on the trip fed Oriental Impressions and Krishna and Radha (Wikipedia); the tour is variously dated 1922-1923, and Encyclopedia.com places the Asian and Near Eastern tour in 1923. Coordinates corrected to the geocode of the Royal Opera House, Girgaon.
stops.campa: The company reaches India and plays the Royal Opera House in Bombay, a baroque theatre built for touring companies out of Europe. Pavlova goes looking, in the cities and outside them, for dancers of the classical Indian traditions, then starved of patronage and despised by the colonial establishment. She watches, takes notes, hires teachers. What she makes of it, Oriental Impressions, is a European's ballet on Indian themes and is criticised as one. It also carries Indian movement onto Western stages years before Indian dancers tour them under their own names.
suggested_refs: The Royal Opera House, Mama Paramanand Marg, Girgaon, Mumbai
Pavlova's Oriental Impressions

stops.name: Rangoon, the colonial stage
stops.date_confidence: attested at country level by Encyclopedia.com, which lists Japan, China, India, Burma and Egypt on the tour; the Rangoon venue and the exact date are reconstruction from the route.
stops.campa: The route goes on into Burma, and the company plays Rangoon: a colonial stage, an orchestra hired locally, a house of British administrators and of Burmese who can pay for seats. That year's tour takes in Japan, China, India, Burma and Egypt, one steamship leg after another with the scenery riding in the hold. She is forty-one. The dancing is not adjusted for the conditions; the conditions are simply what has to be crossed to reach the next town with a theatre in it.
suggested_refs: Colonial theatre circuits of Rangoon in the 1920s

stops.name: Tokyo, the seed of a national tradition
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Japan is attested on the tour by Encyclopedia.com, but the specific venue, the date and the claim that this visit begins Japanese ballet rest on general accounts, not on a documented programme.
stops.campa: The company performs in Tokyo, where classical ballet has no school, no institution and no audience trained to it. Japanese dancers come to watch the technique from the wings. The visit is afterwards named as the beginning of ballet in Japan, an art the country will hold to with more discipline than most of Europe manages. She stays a few weeks. The founding of a national tradition, here as in Peru and Australia, is a by-product of an itinerary drawn up to keep forty people earning.
suggested_refs: Accounts of the beginnings of ballet in Japan following Pavlova's visit

stops.name: Giza, the photograph at the pyramids
stops.date_confidence: attested by the widely reproduced photograph held in multiple archives, including Getty and the V&A Theatre Collections, captioned Pavlova at the pyramids, 1923; the occasion and the surrounding Egyptian dates are not documented in the consulted sources.
stops.campa: Between Asia and Europe the company touches Egypt, and outside Cairo she is photographed at the pyramids in costume, arms lifted, the tombs at her back. The picture runs in illustrated papers around the world and becomes one of the most reproduced images of any dancer. She poses for it deliberately. The photograph goes where the company cannot, into towns with no theatre and no railway, and it sells seats for a season two years off; no agency handles her image, and there is nobody else to do it.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Pavlova at Giza, 1923, Getty Images and V&A Theatre Collections

stops.name: London, Krishna and Radha with Uday Shankar
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia) that she partnered Uday Shankar in a piece titled Krishna and Radha, dated 1923 and placed in London; the venue and the exact performance dates are not given in the consulted sources.
stops.campa: In London she dances Krishna and Radha with Uday Shankar, a young Indian painter studying at the Royal College of Art who has had no training as a dancer at all. She has him build the movement out of temple sculpture and whatever he remembers of home; she learns his gestures and puts the piece into her repertory. Shankar leaves painting for dance and spends the next forty years carrying Indian dance through Europe and America. She is the reason he starts.
suggested_refs: Krishna and Radha, danced by Pavlova and Uday Shankar, 1923

stops.name: Her Majesty's Theatre, Sydney, the Australian opening
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the venue and month: the 1926 Australian and New Zealand tour is attested by Encyclopedia.com and covered in digitised Australian newspapers, but the Sydney opening date and theatre are not confirmed against a programme here.
stops.campa: The company opens in Sydney, the first ballet tour Australia has been given by a dancer of the first rank, and plays to queues around the block. From Sydney the route runs to Melbourne, Adelaide, Perth and across the Tasman to New Zealand. Nothing in the received account of these months marks them out from the ten years of touring before them, except for what the two countries do with her name afterward: within a decade a meringue cake is being served under it in kitchens on both sides of the water.
suggested_refs: National Library of Australia digitised newspaper coverage of the 1926 tour

stops.name: His Majesty's Theatre, Perth, the hotel and the claim
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the tour year is given variously as 1926 or 1929, and the Sachse story is a later Western Australian claim, confirmed by Wikipedia's Pavlova cake article only as a claim, citing The Beverley Times. Coordinates corrected from the Perth city centroid to the theatre at 825 Hay Street.
stops.campa: She plays His Majesty's Theatre in Perth, on the western edge of the continent, the last stop before the Indian Ocean crossing, and stays at the Esplanade Hotel. Nine years later, four years after her death, the hotel's chef Bert Sachse is said to have baked a meringue cake there and named it for her, and Western Australia has held to the story ever since. New Zealand holds to another. The two claims are argued out in cookbooks and newspapers for the rest of the century and are not settled by either.
stops.quote: because it's just not showing up in the cookbooks until really the 1940s in Australia.
stops.quote_source: Helen Leach, culinary anthropologist, rebutting the Sachse claim, quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Pavlova (dessert)'
suggested_refs: The Esplanade Hotel, Perth, and the Bert Sachse claim of 1935

stops.name: Cape Town, the third continent of one year
stops.date_confidence: attested by Encyclopedia.com, which groups the South African tour with Australia and New Zealand in 1926; the research pool's 1928-1929 dating for Cape Town conflicts with that and is not followed. Venue not confirmed; the pin is the Cape Town centroid.
stops.campa: The company plays South Africa, a third continent inside a single touring year, after Australia and New Zealand and before the return to Europe. She is forty-five and has been on the road without a settled season for fifteen years. The programmes are the ones she carries everywhere: national dances, a cut classic, and the swan. Reviewers in every port write the same sentence about her arms, which is the one part of her dancing that will survive in photographs at all.
suggested_refs: South African press notices of the 1926 Pavlova tour

stops.name: Auckland, the recipe takes her name
stops.date_confidence: attested for each individual recipe (Wikipedia, 'Pavlova (dessert)'): a Strawberries Pavlova ice in the New Zealand Herald, 11 November 1911; Emily Futter's meringue with fruit filling, Australia, 1922; a Davis Gelatine jelly called pavlova, Sydney, 1926; the OED's earliest recipe under the name, New Zealand, 1927; Helen Leach's first recognisable pavlova cake, New Zealand, 1929. The origin itself is disputed and unresolved.
stops.campa: The dessert that carries her name is claimed by both countries and traced cleanly by neither. A New Zealand paper prints a Strawberries Pavlova in 1911, but the thing is an ice. An Australian cookbook prints a meringue with fruit filling in 1922. A Sydney gelatine company prints a pavlova in 1926 that turns out to be a layered jelly. The first recognisable meringue cake under the name is found in New Zealand in 1929. Food historians on both sides count recipes and reach different totals. She is dancing on the far side of the world while the name comes loose from her.
stops.quote: pavlova has no singular birthplace. Rather, published recipes reveal the complex process of 'social invention' with practical experience circulating, under a variety of names, across both countries.
stops.quote_source: Michael Symons, food researcher, quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Pavlova (dessert)'
suggested_refs: Helen Leach, The Pavlova Story: A Slice of New Zealand's Culinary History (2008)
New Zealand Herald, 11 November 1911

stops.name: Berlin, the European circuit and the conductor
stops.date_confidence: attested by Encyclopedia.com for a further European tour in 1927 and by Wikipedia for the engagement of Efrem Kurtz as conductor in 1928. Berlin is attested only as a recurring European stop, with no dated appearance confirmed; the pin marks the site of the Kroll Opera House, destroyed in 1943.
stops.campa: She tours Europe again, the continent she now crosses between longer voyages, and engages Efrem Kurtz to conduct for the company. Kurtz holds a travelling pit orchestra together across a dozen countries and as many languages of rehearsal, which is its own kind of dancing. She is approaching fifty and performs the same solos, at the same tempi, that she performed at thirty. Nobody who reviews her in these years reports a decline, which may be accurate and may be the courtesy owed to a monument.
suggested_refs: Efrem Kurtz's engagement as conductor to the Pavlova company, 1928

stops.name: Paris, the last departure north
stops.date_confidence: attested only in the barest form: Wikipedia states that while travelling from Paris to The Hague, Pavlova became ill. The derailment, the unheated carriage and the wet clothes are biographical tradition, repeated in popular accounts and unsupported by the source; no location for any such incident is on record, so no pin is placed for it.
stops.campa: The company plays Paris and then takes the train north for the Netherlands and a season at The Hague. Somewhere on that journey she falls ill. The story that hardens afterward involves a derailment, hours in an unheated carriage and a refusal to change out of wet clothes; the contemporary record says only that she became ill travelling from Paris to The Hague. She arrives with a chill, holds to the rehearsal schedule a day or two longer, and then takes to a bed in a hotel she has stayed in before.
suggested_refs: Contemporary press accounts of the January 1931 journey to The Hague
sources: Keith Money, Anna Pavlova: Her Life and Art (1982)

stops.name: Hotel des Indes, The Hague, the operation refused
stops.date_confidence: attested for the place, the pleurisy and the refused operation (Wikipedia). The date of death is contested: Wikipedia gives 23 January 1931, Encyclopedia.com gives 22 January, and the discrepancy is unresolved. The last words come from Dandre alone and are reported speech, with no second witness.
stops.campa: The chill is pleurisy. The lung fills, the doctors propose to drain it, and they tell her that a rib will have to come out and that she will not dance again. She refuses. Victor Dandre is at the bedside and the company is elsewhere in the city, waiting on a season that will not open. She dies in the small hours, twenty days short of her fiftieth birthday, in the room of a hotel on the Lange Voorhout. Dandre records what she said last, and it is an instruction about a costume.
stops.quote_source: Victor Dandre, Anna Pavlova in Art & Life (1932), p. 360, quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Anna Pavlova'
suggested_refs: Hotel des Indes, 56 Lange Voorhout, The Hague
Obituaries in The Times, January 1931
sources: Victor Dandre, Anna Pavlova in Art & Life (1932)

stops.name: Golders Green Crematorium, the ashes stay in London
stops.date_confidence: attested for the cremation at Golders Green and the placing of the ashes in the columbarium (crematorium records). The ballet shoes said to stand with the urn, and the story of a theft and recovery in the 1980s, appear in no crematorium record and are reconstruction. The exact date of the cremation is not confirmed in the consulted sources.
stops.campa: Her body is cremated at Golders Green, a mile from Ivy House and its lake, and the ashes are placed in the columbarium there rather than carried back to a country that has been the Soviet Union for nine years. Around the urn accrete the stories that attach themselves to relics: that a pair of her ballet shoes stands beside it, that it was stolen once and recovered later. The crematorium's own record mentions neither the shoes nor the theft. What it records is an urn, a name, and a date in January.
suggested_refs: Golders Green Crematorium, 62 Hoop Lane, London NW11 7NL, columbarium records

stops.name: Golders Green, Dandre placed below her
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia) for the death of Victor Dandre on 5 February 1944, his cremation at Golders Green and the placing of his ashes in the columbarium below Pavlova's.
stops.campa: Victor Dandre dies in London in the fifth winter of another war and is placed in the columbarium below her. He had spent thirteen years as keeper of her estate and her reputation, and the memoir he published a year after her death supplies most of what is quoted of her speech, the last words in The Hague included. The book is reprinted in New York in 1979 and is still the only inside account of the household. Everything intimate in the record passes through him, and no second witness stands behind it.
suggested_refs: Victor Dandre, Anna Pavlova in Art & Life (London, 1932; reprinted Arno Press, New York, 1979)

stops.name: Novodevichy Cemetery, Moscow, the return that is called off
stops.date_confidence: attested that a repatriation plan was raised in 2001 with a flight reportedly scheduled for 14 March and then abandoned (British and Russian press coverage; Wikipedia). Who withdrew permission, and why, is reported inconsistently across sources and is not resolved here.
stops.campa: Seventy years after her death Moscow proposes to bring her home. The mayor Yury Luzhkov and a circle of Russian cultural figures arrange to move the ashes to Novodevichy, where the country keeps its artists, and a flight is booked for the fourteenth of March. Objections are raised in Britain, permission is withdrawn on the Russian side, and no document is produced showing that she ever asked to be brought back. The plan is dropped. She stays in north London, a few miles from the house with the lake.
suggested_refs: British and Russian press coverage of the 2001 repatriation dispute

stops.name: Victoria Palace Theatre, the gilded figure restored
stops.date_confidence: attested in theatre heritage accounts that a gilded statue of Pavlova was set on the theatre's cupola at its 1911 opening, removed for safety during the Second World War and lost, and that a replica was restored in 2006. The naming of the algal genus Pavlova is attested by Wikipedia and dated there to the twentieth century, 1952 in the research pool.
stops.campa: A gilded figure of Pavlova is set on the dome of the Victoria Palace Theatre when it opens in 1911, before she has ever danced in the building, because her name on a roofline is worth what it is worth. It comes down for safety in the Second World War and is lost. In 2006 a replica goes back up over Victoria Street. A genus of microscopic marine algae also carries her name, given for the way the cells move through water, which one describer calls positively balletic.
suggested_refs: Victoria Palace Theatre heritage records on the Pavlova statue and its 2006 replica
The algal genus Pavlova
